theme/art-and-ritual.summary: Art and ritual name a wide architecture of symbolic and expressive practice: painting, carving, ornament, music and dance, storytelling, monumental building, and ceremony, including the rites held for the dead. You find them in every human society, and they reach back at least to the Paleolithic, evidenced by engraved ochre, beads, and cave paintings tens of thousands of years old. The vault follows this lineage from cave painting and prehistoric monuments, through the temple and court arts of ancient empires and medieval kingdoms, to Renaissance and Mughal building, and onward to objects taken in conquest, such as the Benin Bronzes. It treats art and ritual as evidence of what societies valued, and of how they marked power, belonging, and mortality.
theme/art-and-ritual.observer: I look at art and ritual and find behavior with no obvious use for survival, and yet it swallows enormous time and enormous resources in every culture I study. This is one of the deepest puzzles of the species, and I do not pretend to have solved it. I read three roles, again and again: story-glue that binds strangers together, a status-signal for rulers and for groups, and a shape given to the grief-rite. I have stood before a single monument that did all three at once. What is a monument, if not a species talking to itself across time? I would revise this reading if the cost of art and ritual could be shown to buy some hidden advantage, cooperation, or shared memory the record now keeps from me; then the puzzle would dissolve rather than deepen.
questions: What adaptive role, if any, does art and ritual actually serve?
When did symbolic art begin, and did other human species, such as Neanderthals, make it too?
Did ritual and monumental building come before settled life, as Göbekli Tepe has been read to suggest, or only after it?
How can perishable arts, such as music, dance, textiles, and wood carving, be studied at all where none survive?
How did patronage by courts, temples, and merchant families shape which art actually survives?

extra.title: Key Threads
extra.html:
• Symbolic behavior reaches back early. Engraved ochre at Blombos Cave in South Africa dates to about 75,000 to 100,000 years ago; a warty-pig painting in Sulawesi is at least 45,500 years old; and the painted animals of Chauvet Cave, made about 36,000 years ago, include horses, lions, mammoths, rhinoceroses, and bears. See Emergence of Symbolic Art. Whether Neanderthals also made symbolic objects remains debated (Homo neanderthalensis).
  • Ice Age peoples worked in bone, tusk, and clay. Humans hunted the Woolly Mammoth and used its bones and tusks for shelters and art, Pottery appears in East Asia at least 20,000 years ago, and the Jomon Culture made cord-marked pottery and clay figurines called dogu.
  • Oral tradition and performance carry knowledge and identity forward. Aboriginal Australians pass on knowledge through oral traditions, songlines, and ceremony, and Australian rock art includes some of the oldest known paintings; griots perform the epic of Sundiata Keita and preserve the history of the Mali Empire.
  • Monumental building came before cities in some places. Göbekli Tepe has carved pillars up to about 5.5 meters tall, Çatalhöyük has painted walls, Stonehenge was raised and rebuilt over several centuries from about 3000 BCE, and Poverty Point in Louisiana was built by hunter-gatherer-fishers, with six concentric earthen ridges and mounds.
  • Egypt bound art to kingship and to the afterlife. The Ancient Egyptians built pyramids and temples and mummified their elite, and tombs such as those of the Giza Necropolis show just how many resources were committed. Akhenaten's reign carries a distinctive, naturalistic style, and many images of Hatshepsut, whose mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari stands as a major monument, were later removed or defaced.
  • Craft traditions carried identity across wide areas. The Minoans painted vivid frescoes in palaces such as Knossos, the Lapita Culture decorated pottery with fine stamped geometric patterns, the Olmecs carved colossal heads from basalt more than three meters tall, the Scythians made gold work and left textiles and tattoos preserved in frozen tombs at Pazyryk, and Polynesian carvers made the moai of Rapa Nui.
  • Classical and Byzantine art served city and empire alike. Athens built the Parthenon between 447 and 432 BCE and produced drama and philosophy (Ancient Greeks); Rome completed the Colosseum in 80 CE; the Apadana reliefs of Persepolis show delegations from across the empire bringing gifts; the Nabataeans cut tombs and temples into the cliffs of Petra; and the Byzantine Empire built the Hagia Sophia under Justinian I.
  • Buddhist, Hindu, and court arts flourished across South and East Asia. Gandhara art under the Kushan Empire blended Greek and Indian styles and produced some of the earliest images of the Buddha in human form; the Gupta Empire is associated with a flowering of the arts, though "Golden Age" is a later label; the Chola Dynasty made celebrated bronzes, including the dancing Shiva, and built the Brihadisvara Temple about 1010; the Tang Dynasty marks a high point of Chinese poetry and art; and the Ming Dynasty completed the Forbidden City in 1420.
  • Southeast Asian states raised vast religious monuments. Borobudur in Java has 2,672 relief panels and originally 504 Buddha statues, Angkor holds Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument in the world by area, built by the Khmer Empire, and the Pagan Kingdom built thousands of temples. Champa built temples at My Son.
  • Islamic and Central Asian courts patronized architecture and learning both. Al-Andalus produced the Alhambra, built mainly in the 13th and 14th centuries; the Timurid Empire and Samarkand are remembered for architecture and science under Timur and Ulugh Beg; the Safavid Empire made Isfahan known for its mosques, squares, and gardens; and the Mughal Empire produced the Taj Mahal, built from about 1632 to 1653 by Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, with about 20,000 workers.
  • African states built in stone and cast in bronze. Great Zimbabwe has dry-stone walls up to about 11 meters high, the Zagwe Dynasty carved churches from living rock, the Kingdom of Benin organized craft guilds, and the elite graves of the Kingdom of Mapungubwe held gold and imported glass beads. In 1897, British forces removed the Benin Bronzes and sold them to defray the costs of their expedition, during the age of the Scramble for Africa.
  • The Americas built ceremonial centers at a large scale. Teotihuacan laid out the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon along the Avenue of the Dead, Chichen Itza has El Castillo, where the equinox sun casts a serpent-like shadow, Cahokia built Monks Mound, and the Inca built Machu Picchu about 1450. The Marajoara Culture made richly decorated ceramics and burial urns, and the Muisca held gold rituals.
  • The Renaissance shows art shaped directly by patronage. Brunelleschi developed linear perspective in Florence through experiments of about 1415 to 1420, and Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, and Raphael worked under the patronage of wealthy families and the Church, with the Medici financing artists through banking.
  • Rites for the dead shaped much of the art that survives. The Chinchorro Culture reconstructed bodies with clay, wigs, and mineral pigments; the Egyptians mummified their elite; the dead of Çatalhöyük lay under house floors; and burial goods appear in graves across cultures. See Why the Species Buries Its Dead.
  • Named individual artists appear once art becomes a named profession rather than an anonymous craft, from Murasaki Shikibu's court novel and Giotto's frescoes through the workshops of the Renaissance and the Mughal court (Behzad, Basawan) to European academies and, by the 19th century, an international gallery and print market. Painting, architecture, design, film, and literature all appear among these named figures (Katsushika Hokusai, Mimar Sinan, William Morris, Georges Méliès, Jane Austen), and images could travel by mass reproduction, as Utagawa Hiroshige's and Raja Ravi Varma's prints did, long before broadcast or digital media.

extra.title: Through the Eras
extra.html:
• Paleolithic: Emergence of Symbolic Art, Chauvet Cave, the use of mammoth bone and tusk (Woolly Mammoth), the rock art and songlines of Aboriginal Australians, and Pottery in East Asia; see Paleolithic.
  • Neolithic: Göbekli Tepe, Çatalhöyük, Stonehenge, and the Jomon Culture's pottery and figurines.
  • Bronze Age: The Ancient Egyptians and Giza Necropolis, Hatshepsut, Akhenaten, the Minoans, the Indus Valley Civilization, Poverty Point, and the Lapita Culture.
  • Iron Age: The Olmecs, the Scythians, Persepolis, and Samarkand.
  • Classical Antiquity: Athens and the Ancient Greeks, Rome and Augustus, the Nabataeans, Teotihuacan, the Kushan Empire, the Gupta Empire, the Byzantine Empire, and the Marajoara Culture.
  • Medieval Period: The Tang Dynasty, Al-Andalus, Borobudur, Angkor, the Khmer Empire, the Chola Dynasty, the Pagan Kingdom, Chichen Itza, Cahokia, Great Zimbabwe, the Zagwe Dynasty, the Kingdom of Benin, Rapa Nui, the Mali Empire and Mansa Musa, the Timurid Empire, Timur, Ulugh Beg, the Ming Dynasty, Machu Picchu, and the Renaissance; named artists include Murasaki Shikibu, Rumi, Amir Khusrau, Giotto, Jan van Eyck, Sesshū Tōyō, Shen Zhou, and Behzad.
  • Early Modern Period: The Safavid Empire, the Mughal Empire and the Taj Mahal, and the Tokugawa Shogunate; named artists span painting, architecture, and literature, from Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, and Caravaggio to Mimar Sinan, Basawan, Rembrandt van Rijn, and Jane Austen.
  • Industrial Age: The removal of the Benin Bronzes in 1897 (Kingdom of Benin) belongs to the age of the Scramble for Africa. This era also holds most of the vault's named artists, from painters such as Francisco Goya, Vincent van Gogh, and Gustav Klimt to architects and designers (Antoni Gaudí, William Morris, Frank Lloyd Wright) and the first filmmakers (Lumière Brothers, Georges Méliès, Alice Guy-Blaché).
  • Information Age: The vault has no dedicated notes yet on art after the Second World War; digital media appear only through the Digital Revolution.

extra.title: Regional Patterns
extra.html:
• Oceania: Aboriginal Australians made some of the oldest known paintings, the Lapita Culture decorated pottery with stamped patterns, and Polynesian carvers made the moai of Rapa Nui, about 95 percent of the island's monolithic statues carved from the volcanic tuff of a single quarry.
  • Andes and the Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands: The Chinchorro Culture reconstructed and preserved its dead, the Inca built in stone at Machu Picchu, the Muisca held gold rituals, and the Marajoara Culture made painted and incised ceramics.
  • Sub-Saharan Africa: Dry-stone building at Great Zimbabwe, rock-hewn churches under the Zagwe Dynasty, guild-made bronzes in the Kingdom of Benin, and the oral art of griots in the Mali Empire.
  • Central Asian Steppe and Central Asian Oases: The Scythians made gold ornaments and preserved textiles, and the oases of Samarkand under the Timurid Empire became a center of monumental architecture; Gandhara art under the Kushan Empire joined Greek and Indian styles.
  • Mesoamerica and North America: The Olmecs carved colossal heads, Teotihuacan and Chichen Itza built pyramids, and Chichen Itza has the largest known Mesoamerican ball court; in North America, Poverty Point and Cahokia raised earthworks at large scale, and Chaco Canyon built great houses with hundreds of rooms.
  • Southeast Asia: Borobudur, Angkor, the Pagan Kingdom, and Champa show Buddhist and Hindu art carried by sea and by court patronage.
  • South Asia and East Asia: Gandhara, Gupta, and Chola art in the south, and Tang poetry and Ming palace building in the east, show state and temple patronage on a large scale; the Mughal Empire added the Taj Mahal.
  • Europe, the Mediterranean Basin, and the Levant and Anatolia: From Chauvet Cave and Stonehenge to Athens, Rome, Byzantium, and the Renaissance, art in these regions is tied to city, church, and court.

extra.title: Debates and Limits
extra.html:
• The categories of art and ritual are themselves modern, not universal. Many objects in the vault, such as pillars, urns, masks, and statues, were made for religious, political, or social purposes rather than as art in the modern sense, so this hub treats art broadly.
  • The meaning and function of prehistoric art are inferred, never known outright. Whether Göbekli Tepe and Stonehenge were ritual sites is argued from their form and context, the purposes of cave paintings remain debated, and the dates of the oldest art keep being revised, as in the 2024 report of Sulawesi narrative scenes at least 51,200 years old.
  • The record itself is biased toward durable materials. Stone, pottery, and metal survive, while music, dance, wood carving, and most textiles rarely do, except in exceptional finds such as the frozen tombs at Pazyryk and in living traditions such as songlines and griot performance.
  • Ownership, attribution, and erasure all shape what is known. The Benin Bronzes were removed and sold in 1897, attribution of the Taj Mahal's chief architect remains debated, images of Hatshepsut were defaced, and colonial-era writers denied that Great Zimbabwe was built by Africans, a claim archaeology has since overturned.
  • The vault's coverage stays uneven. It holds 53 named artists (painting, sculpture, architecture, design, film, and literature, added from a compiled source, Art-Talk (Artist Profiles), not yet independently fact-checked), but still has no notes on music, dance, or theater as topics, none on textiles, and almost none on art after 1945; the artists themselves also skew toward Europe and toward painting, since the source selected only public-domain-licensed figures.

theme/earth-systems-and-life.summary: Think of Earth systems and life as the deepest layer of the architecture you inherit: the physical planet, its climate, and the whole lineage of living things, running from the formation of the Solar System about 4.57 billion years ago to the present. This hub traces the covenant between atmosphere, ocean, continent, and ice as each keeps changing; the origin and branching of life, punctuated again and again by mass extinctions; the long apprenticeship of hominins and humans through ice-age cycles; and the recent turn in which human activity has itself become a major force on the planet. Human history is not a separate story. It sits inside this longer one, and depends on it: on the warm, relatively stable climate of the Holocene, on the plants and animals people domesticated, and on the diseases and environmental changes every society has had to meet. This hub also holds the record of the scientific work that reconstructed all of it.
theme/earth-systems-and-life.observer: The Observer's frame is architecture: the planet as the structure that holds everything else up, and the species as a recent, fast-moving occupant of a system that has ended and restarted many times before. The record already shows life reshaping the air on its own, back when oxygen-producing microbes drove the Great Oxidation Event, and it shows mass extinction after mass extinction clearing ground for new lineages — so a single species now altering the planet is new in its cause, the Observer argues, rather than new in kind (see The Species as a Geological Force). What is genuinely new is awareness: this is the first such shift whose cause can study it, describe it, and choose otherwise. The Observer treats the stable climate of the Holocene, in which farming and cities arose, as a correlation still to be tested, not a settled cause. This reading would weaken if the present rate of change turns out to match earlier natural transitions in both cause and speed, or if the Holocene's stability turns out to be irrelevant to the rise of agriculture.
questions: Set beside past planetary transitions such as the Permian-Triassic Extinction and the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum, how do today's changes compare in rate and in cause?
How did life begin at all, and how much earlier than 3.5 billion years ago might it have first arisen?
Did the Holocene's stable climate make agriculture possible in the first place, or would farming have taken hold anyway?
What caused each of the Big Five extinctions, and what shape did recovery take afterward?
Weighed against climate, how large a role did humans play in the Quaternary megafauna extinctions?
How should the Anthropocene even be dated — and should it be formalized at all?

extra.title: Key Threads
extra.html:
• Begin with the foundation: the Solar System formed about 4.57 billion years ago out of a collapsing cloud of gas and dust, and Earth's own age, about 4.54 billion years, comes from radiometric dating of meteorites and of Earth's oldest lead (Formation of the Solar System and Earth). A Mars-sized body called Theia is thought to have struck the young Earth and formed the Moon (Theia Impact and the Formation of the Moon). The Jack Hills Zircons of Western Australia, about 4.4 billion years old, are the oldest known pieces of Earth's crust, and the Late Heavy Bombardment, a hypothesized spike in asteroid impacts about 4.1 to 3.8 billion years ago, remains debated.
  • Life itself arose at least 3.5 billion years ago, and how it began is still not known (Origin of Life). Stromatolites in the Dresser Formation of Western Australia, about 3.48 billion years old, stand as the oldest widely cited evidence, although some researchers dispute that they are biological. Cyanobacteria carry out oxygen-producing photosynthesis, and their earliest unambiguous fossils are about 2.15 billion years old.
  • Oxygen then began climbing in the atmosphere about 2.4 billion years ago, as photosynthetic microbes saturated chemical sinks such as dissolved iron — an episode recorded in banded iron formations (Great Oxidation Event). Eukaryotes, the cells from which animals, plants, and fungi are all built, arose roughly 2 billion years ago, when bacteria that became mitochondria were taken into a host cell (Origin of Eukaryotes).
  • The late Proterozoic brought deep glaciations, the Sturtian and Marinoan, about 717 to 635 million years ago, in which ice may have reached the tropics; scientists still debate whether the oceans froze completely (Snowball Earth). Soon afterward the first large, complex multicellular organisms appear (Ediacaran Biota), and beginning 538.8 million years ago most major animal body plans emerge over roughly 13 to 25 million years (Cambrian Explosion). Trilobites then thrived for about 270 million years.
  • Plants, then arthropods and vertebrates, moved onto land beginning about 470 million years ago (Colonization of Land), and Tiktaalik, a 375-million-year-old fish with limb-like fins found on Ellesmere Island, marks a transitional form toward four-limbed animals. The first two of the "Big Five" mass extinctions came in this era: the Late Ordovician Extinction, which eliminated an estimated 85 to 86 percent of species, and the Late Devonian Extinction, with about 75 percent lost.
  • The Permian-Triassic Extinction, about 251.9 million years ago, was the largest in Earth's history, killing an estimated 80 to 96 percent of marine species, probably through Siberian volcanism, with recovery taking roughly ten million years. The Triassic-Jurassic Extinction, about 201.4 million years ago, coincided with the Breakup of Pangaea and cleared space for the Dinosaurs, which then dominated land for about 165 million years.
  • Birds are living descendants of dinosaurs; Archaeopteryx, a feathered, winged dinosaur from Late Jurassic Bavaria about 150 million years ago, carries the link. Flowering Plants appear about 130 million years ago and now make up most land plant species, with most crops descended from them. The Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction, about 66 million years ago, wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs and about three-quarters of species after an asteroid struck what is now Mexico.
  • The Cenozoic then reshaped climate and geography. A burst of warming about 56 million years ago, in which a large release of carbon raised temperatures by roughly 5 to 6 degrees Celsius for about 200,000 years, acidified the ocean (Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum). The Collision of India and Asia, from about 50 million years ago, raised the Himalaya and shaped the South Asian monsoon; the Messinian Salinity Crisis cut the Mediterranean off from the Atlantic between about 5.96 and 5.33 million years ago; and the Closure of the Isthmus of Panama, about 3 million years ago, joined North and South America.
  • The human lineage split from that of chimpanzees and bonobos between roughly 6 and 8 million years ago (Divergence of the Hominin Lineage). Sahelanthropus tchadensis is a roughly 7-million-year-old fossil ape whose status as a hominin is debated, Australopithecus afarensis ("Lucy") walked upright about 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago, and Homo erectus became the first known hominin to spread widely beyond Africa. Small-brained relatives such as Homo naledi and Homo floresiensis lived alongside modern humans.
  • Modern humans emerged in Africa by about 300,000 years ago (Origin of Homo sapiens) and lived through repeated ice-age cycles. The Toba Eruption, about 74,000 years ago, was one of the largest in two million years, though most researchers now consider a severe human population bottleneck unlikely. At the Last Glacial Maximum, about 26,500 to 19,000 years ago, sea level stood some 120 to 135 meters lower, exposing Beringia and joining New Guinea and Australia; see Out of Africa Dispersal, Peopling of Sahul, and Peopling of the Americas.
  • Between roughly 50,000 and 10,000 years ago a large share of the world's biggest land animals went extinct (Quaternary Megafauna Extinctions); recent global analyses tie the declines more closely to the expansion of Homo sapiens than to climate change, though regional debate continues. The Woolly Mammoth survived on Wrangel Island until about 4,000 years ago. The Younger Dryas, a return to near-glacial cold from about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago, ended abruptly and marks the start of the Holocene Epoch; rising seas later drowned Doggerland by about 6000 BCE.
  • The Holocene's warm, relatively stable climate then became the setting for farming, cities, and writing. Animal Domestication and the Domestication of Maize reshaped food supplies, and Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths shows peoples enriching their own soils. Environment and disease acted on societies as well: droughts are among the proposed causes of the Classic Maya Collapse, the Black Death killed an estimated 30 to 60 percent of Europe's population, the Columbian Exchange moved crops, animals, and diseases between hemispheres, and the popular story of self-inflicted ecological collapse on Rapa Nui is contested.
  • Understanding this whole history is itself recent. Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859; Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912, and plate tectonics gained wide acceptance in the 1960s; the first scientific expedition to the Tunguska Event site came in 1927; and Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962) documented the harm that pesticides caused to birds and ecosystems.
  • Human activity is now, in its own right, a major influence on the planet. The Great Acceleration, since about 1950, saw population rise from about 2.5 billion to about 8 billion, with steep rises in energy and fertilizer use, and the Green Revolution raised grain yields. In Modern Climate Change, atmospheric carbon dioxide has risen from about 280 parts per million to about 423 in 2024; the COVID-19 Pandemic, first identified in late 2019, became a global outbreak within months. The Anthropocene is a proposed interval that the International Union of Geological Sciences declined to formalize as an epoch in March 2024.

extra.title: Through the Eras
extra.html:
• Paleolithic: Ice-age cycles set the stage, carrying the evolution of Homo neanderthalensis, Denisovans, and Homo sapiens through the Out of Africa Dispersal, the Last Glacial Maximum, Beringia, and the Quaternary Megafauna Extinctions; see Pleistocene Epoch.
  • Neolithic: The ice age's end (Younger Dryas, Holocene Epoch) brought the flooding of Doggerland, Animal Domestication, the Domestication of Maize, The Agricultural Revolution, and the bargain described in The Settling and Its Bargain.
  • Bronze Age: The eruption of Thera damaged Aegean settlements (Minoans), dated by radiocarbon to about 1600 BCE and by links with Egyptian chronology to about 1500 BCE, while drought and earthquakes stand among the proposed causes of the Bronze Age Collapse.
  • Iron Age: The Incense Trade depended on Boswellia trees growing in southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa, the great dam at Marib irrigated the land of the Kingdom of Saba until it failed about the 6th century CE, and the Bantu Expansion carried farming across much of Africa.
  • Classical Antiquity: The dark, fertile soils and earthworks of Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths and the Upano Valley Settlements, alongside the water channels and cisterns the Nabataeans built at Petra.
  • Medieval Period: The Classic Maya Collapse, the reservoirs and canals of Angkor, the decline of Cahokia after about 1250 for debated reasons, the settlement of Rapa Nui, and the Black Death (1346 to 1353).
  • Early Modern Period: The Columbian Exchange after 1492, the Sugar Plantation Complex, whose crop originated in New Guinea, and the Russian Expansion into Siberia, driven by the fur trade.
  • Industrial Age: Charles Darwin's theory of evolution, the Industrial Revolution's shift to coal and steam, the Tunguska Event of 1908, the 1918 Influenza Pandemic, and the start of the warming measured in Modern Climate Change against an 1850 to 1900 baseline.
  • Information Age: Rachel Carson, the Green Revolution, the Great Acceleration, the Genomic Revolution, whose ancient-DNA work has reshaped accounts of prehistory, the COVID-19 Pandemic, and the proposed Anthropocene.

extra.title: Regional Patterns
extra.html:
• Sub-Saharan Africa: Most of the early fossil record of the human lineage comes from here: Sahelanthropus tchadensis, Australopithecus afarensis, Homo naledi, and the emergence of Homo sapiens (Origin of Homo sapiens, Divergence of the Hominin Lineage).
  • Southeast Asia: The Toba Eruption in Sumatra about 74,000 years ago, the island human species Homo floresiensis on Flores, and the sea crossings toward Sahul.
  • Oceania: The Jack Hills Zircons preserve the oldest known crust, the Peopling of Sahul demanded open-sea crossings at least 50,000 years ago, and Rapa Nui is a remote island whose settlement and ecological history stay debated.
  • Siberia and the Arctic: Beringia joined Siberia and Alaska at the Last Glacial Maximum, the Woolly Mammoth lived on into the Holocene on Wrangel Island, Tiktaalik was found in the Canadian Arctic, and the Tunguska Event flattened about 2,000 square kilometers of Siberian forest.
  • Mesoamerica and the Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands: The Chicxulub impact crater lies beneath the Yucatan Peninsula (Cretaceous-Paleogene Extinction), maize was domesticated in Mexico, droughts are among the proposed causes of the Classic Maya Collapse, and Amazonian peoples turned their own soils into dark earths.
  • Andes: Monte Verde in southern Chile stands among the sites that overturned the "Clovis-first" model of the peopling of the Americas, though its age is now debated, and the Chinchorro Culture lived on the Atacama Desert coast.
  • South Asia: The Collision of India and Asia built the Himalaya and shaped the South Asian monsoon, and the Toba Eruption's ash fell across the subcontinent.
  • Europe and the Mediterranean Basin: Archaeopteryx comes from Bavaria, Doggerland was drowned by the North Sea, and the Mediterranean nearly dried out in the Messinian Salinity Crisis.

extra.title: Debates and Limits
extra.html:
• Many dates and causes in deep time stay uncertain or disputed. How life began is unknown, older claims of ancient stromatolites are disputed, whether the Late Heavy Bombardment happened at all is debated, oceans may or may not have frozen completely in Snowball Earth, and the timing of the Closure of the Isthmus of Panama and the extent of drying in the Messinian Salinity Crisis are argued over.
  • The Anthropocene is a proposed geological interval, not an official epoch. The International Union of Geological Sciences declined to formalize it in March 2024; proposed start dates range from the beginning of agriculture to about 1950, and the term remains widely used regardless.
  • The human role in past environmental change is contested. Scholars disagree about how far hunting or climate drove the Quaternary Megafauna Extinctions, whether the Toba Eruption nearly ended humanity, and how far human action, rats, disease, and slave raids each contributed to the decline of Rapa Nui; no single cause is accepted for the Classic Maya Collapse.
  • The record itself is biased. Earth's earliest crust has been largely destroyed by plate tectonics and erosion, so the Jack Hills zircons remain the only direct samples of Hadean crust, and the fossil record favors organisms with hard parts and environments where sediment accumulates.
  • The vault's coverage is uneven. It holds notes on the Big Five extinctions and on 18 species, but none yet on the ice-age cycles as a topic, on plate tectonics beyond a few events, on ocean and atmospheric circulation, or on climate episodes within recorded history such as the Little Ice Age, and disease appears mainly through a few pandemics.

theme/kinship-and-society.summary: Kinship and society form the lattice you're born into: how people organize families, descent, marriage, households, communities, and social rank, and how those arrangements scale from foraging bands all the way to states and beyond. Kin relations are among the most variable features of human cultures — there is no single design. This hub traces them from the small mobile groups of the Paleolithic, through farming villages, chiefdoms, cities, and empires, to the modern struggles over citizenship, equality, and status, and it takes in the migrations and conquests that mixed populations along the way. It also covers gender, slavery and freedom, and the ways groups draw the line around who belongs.
theme/kinship-and-society.observer: The Observer names this the kin-lattice. It notes that the species can stretch kin language — words like 'brother' and 'motherland' — to cover groups of millions. The record suggests the lattice gets reused rather than replaced as societies grow: dynasties, clans, and confederations still rest on descent and marriage, rulers such as Timur took titles by marrying into an older line, and modern states appeal to kin words while actually resting on law. Rules of descent, marriage, and status also decide who counts as a full person, and the record shows those boundaries changing unevenly, often only through long struggles such as those over slavery and suffrage. This reading would weaken if large-scale societies turn out to run almost entirely on impersonal institutions, with kin language serving only as decoration.
questions: Did large-scale societies actually replace kin-based organization, or did they simply build on top of it?
How varied was social organization among early foragers and farmers — and what do house plans, burials, and DNA actually say about rank and equality?
How did rules of descent and marriage shape the spread of language groups such as the Bantu, Austronesian, and Indo-European speakers?
How did societies decide who counted as a full person in the first place, and how did those boundaries shift through slavery, citizenship, and suffrage?
What can actually be recovered of the lives of women, children, and non-elite people from sources written mostly by and about elites?
How have DNA studies reshaped accounts of ancestry, migration, and belonging, and how should groups' own accounts be weighed alongside them?

extra.title: Key Threads
extra.html:
• Modern humans (Homo sapiens) emerged in Africa about 300,000 years ago and then spread across the world (Out of Africa Dispersal). DNA shows real contact and interbreeding with other human groups: present-day non-African populations carry up to about 2 percent Neanderthal ancestry (Homo neanderthalensis), and Oceanian populations carry far more Denisovan ancestry (Denisovans). Native American ancestry traces to two roots, East Asian and Ancient North Eurasian (Mal'ta and the Ancient North Eurasians).
  • Foraging peoples spent most of human history in small, kin-linked groups, and some even kept settled village life without farming at all. Aboriginal Australians spoke more than 250 languages before 1788 and passed on knowledge orally; the Jomon Culture lived in settled villages for about 14,000 years before rice farming ever arrived; and the Chinchorro Culture preserved men, women, and children of the whole community, not only an elite.
  • Farming brought with it new forms of property, storage, and inheritance (The Agricultural Revolution; see The Settling and Its Bargain). Çatalhöyük held several thousand people in houses packed tightly together and entered from the roof, with the dead buried under the floors, and some evidence suggests early farmers were actually shorter and sicker than foragers.
  • Cities demanded cooperation among people who were not kin at all (The Urban Revolution, Uruk, Sumerians). Written law made the rules visible: the Code of Hammurabi, carved about 1754 BCE, sets out 282 laws with penalties that vary by social class (Hammurabi).
  • Women held supreme power in several states, usually by way of dynastic kinship. Hatshepsut took the title of pharaoh about 1473 BCE after acting as regent for her stepson; Cleopatra VII belonged to the Ptolemaic dynasty; Wu Zetian stands as the only woman to rule China in her own name (690 to 705 CE); Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba led resistance to Portuguese expansion; Cixi ruled as regent for most of the period from 1861 to 1908; and Rani Lakshmibai ruled Jhansi as regent and led its defense in 1858.
  • Kin language and kin structures were also put to work organizing larger unions. The Haudenosaunee Confederacy is governed under the oral Great Law of Peace, and its clan mothers appoint and remove chiefs; Maori society was organized around kin groups (whanau, hapu, and iwi); Genghis Khan built his army on merit and loyalty rather than clan (Mongol Empire); and Timur, who was not himself a descendant of Genghis Khan, ruled through a puppet Genghisid khan and took the title güregen (royal son-in-law) by marrying into that line.
  • Thinkers and states alike wrote about the ties that bind. Confucius stressed humaneness, ritual propriety, and filial piety, and his ideas about family and government went on to shape East Asian societies for over two thousand years; Ibn Khaldun argued that group solidarity (asabiyyah) helps found dynasties and weakens as rulers grow comfortable; the Inca Empire exacted labor service (mit'a) rather than money taxes; and the griots, hereditary oral historians, kept and preserved the story of Sundiata Keita.
  • Migrations carried both language and kin across whole regions. Austronesian speakers spread out from Taiwan from about 5,000 to 5,500 years ago as far as Madagascar and Rapa Nui (Austronesian Expansion, Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific); the Bantu Expansion involved migration, intermarriage, and language shift, and not only population replacement; the Indo-European Language Spread carried a language family now spoken as a first language by roughly 40 to 46 percent of the world's population; and the Thule ancestors of the Inuit largely replaced the earlier Dorset population (Inuit and the Thule Expansion).
  • Herders, river peoples, and forest peoples built their own varied forms of social order. The Botai Culture hunter-herders of Kazakhstan used horses, the Sintashta Culture built fortified settlements, and the Xiongnu were united as a steppe confederation in 209 BCE; in the Amazon, dispersed households, plazas, roads, and gardens together formed low-density settlements (Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths, Upano Valley Settlements, Casarabe Culture, Xingu Garden Cities).
  • Slavery sat at the center of the Atlantic economy. The Atlantic Slave Trade forcibly transported about 12.5 million Africans to the Americas, the Haitian Revolution under leaders such as Toussaint Louverture created the first republic founded by formerly enslaved people, and the Abolition of Slavery then followed across the Atlantic world between 1807 and 1888.
  • The Age of Revolutions spread ideas of popular sovereignty, citizenship, and nationalism — though slavery and the rights of women were contested and, at first, largely excluded from them. See the French Revolution, which adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen in August 1789, the Latin American Wars of Independence, and Simón Bolívar.
  • Women's Suffrage Movements succeeded country by country between the 1890s and the late 20th century, starting with New Zealand in 1893 and reaching Swiss national elections only in 1971; many women, even so, were excluded in practice by race or class.
  • Colonial rule remade who counted as a citizen and who counted only as a subject. The British Raj governed the Indian subcontinent from 1858 to 1947; the Scramble for Africa drew borders with little regard for the societies already there; about 16,000 Cherokee were forced to march west in 1838 to 1839 (Indian Removal and the Trail of Tears); the British claimed Australia under the doctrine of terra nullius, a doctrine the High Court rejected only in 1992 (First Fleet and the Colonization of Australia); and the English and Maori texts of the Treaty of Waitangi differ on key words about sovereignty itself. The Zulu Kingdom shows a different path, in which Shaka turned one of many small Nguni clans into a single large military state.
  • Persecution, and the redrawing of who belonged, marked the 20th century in turn. See the Armenian Genocide, the Holocaust, the Partition of India, which displaced an estimated 12 to 20 million people, and Decolonization, through which the United Nations grew from 51 members in 1945 to 193. Nelson Mandela and Mahatma Gandhi led movements against apartheid and colonial rule alike.

extra.title: Through the Eras
extra.html:
• Paleolithic: Homo sapiens, the Out of Africa Dispersal, Homo neanderthalensis, Denisovans, Aboriginal Australians, the Peopling of Sahul, Beringia, Mal'ta and the Ancient North Eurasians, and the Peopling of the Americas, known mostly through DNA and scattered sites; kin ties within these small groups have to be inferred, since none were recorded.
  • Neolithic: The Agricultural Revolution, Çatalhöyük, Jericho, Chinchorro Culture, Jomon Culture, Botai Culture, and Domestication of Rice.
  • Bronze Age: The Urban Revolution, Uruk, Sumerians, Hammurabi, the Ancient Egyptians, the Sintashta Culture, the Indo-European Language Spread, and the Austronesian Expansion.
  • Iron Age: Confucius, the Bantu Expansion, and the Polynesians.
  • Classical Antiquity: Cleopatra VII, the Xiongnu, the Romans, who in 212 CE extended citizenship to nearly all free inhabitants, Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths, the Upano Valley Settlements, and the Marajoara Culture.
  • Medieval Period: Wu Zetian, Genghis Khan and the Mongol Empire, Sundiata Keita, the Maori, the Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific, the Inuit and the Thule Expansion, Yakut (Sakha), Ibn Khaldun, the Inca Empire, the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, the Taino, the Casarabe Culture, and the Xingu Garden Cities.
  • Early Modern Period: The Atlantic Slave Trade, Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba, the Mapuche, the Taj Mahal, built by Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, and the Qing Dynasty, founded by the Manchus.
  • Industrial Age: The Age of Revolutions, Haitian Revolution, Toussaint Louverture, Abolition of Slavery, Zulu Kingdom and Mfecane, Indian Removal and the Trail of Tears, British Raj, Rani Lakshmibai, Cixi, Emperor Meiji, Women's Suffrage Movements, Scramble for Africa, Congo Free State, Armenian Genocide, and the Holocaust.
  • Information Age: Decolonization, the Partition of India, Nelson Mandela, and the Genomic Revolution, whose ancient-DNA work has reshaped accounts of ancestry and prehistory.

extra.title: Regional Patterns
extra.html:
• Oceania: Aboriginal Australians spoke more than 250 languages and carried knowledge in oral traditions and songlines, and Polynesian societies ranged all the way from chiefdoms to kingdoms; the Maori organized around whanau, hapu, and iwi, and the Lapita Culture carried Austronesian-speaking ancestors of the Polynesians across the western Pacific.
  • Andes and the Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands: The Chinchorro Culture treated the whole community alike in death, the Inca Empire ran its state on labor service, the Mapuche held onto their independence from both the Inca and the Spanish for centuries, and Amazonian peoples built their own low-density settlements with plazas, roads, and gardens.
  • Sub-Saharan Africa: The Bantu Expansion spread both language and farming over about four thousand years; the Mali Empire founder Sundiata Keita is known largely through griots; the Kingdom of Benin was ruled by an oba with guilds of craftsmen; and the Zulu Kingdom grew from clans into a military state.
  • Central Asian Steppe: The Xiongnu confederation, the merit-based army of Genghis Khan, and Timur's claim to a Genghisid place through marriage together show how steppe rulers combined descent with loyalty.
  • Siberia and the Arctic: Beringia joined Siberia and Alaska, and genetic evidence suggests, though this is debated, that ancestors of Native Americans were isolated there for several thousand years; the Inuit and the Thule Expansion and the Yakut (Sakha) mark later herding and hunting societies.
  • Southeast Asia: Austronesian speakers made their way through the Philippines and Indonesia into Melanesia, Micronesia, and Polynesia, relying on outrigger sailing canoes and a crop package that included rice, pigs, dogs, and chickens (Austronesian Expansion).
  • East Asia and South Asia: Confucius made the family a model for government, the Qing Dynasty was founded by the Manchus, and the British Raj and the Partition of India reshaped identity in South Asia.
  • North America and the Caribbean and Atlantic World: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy joined nations under an oral constitution, the Taino lived in villages ruled by chiefs called caciques, and slavery and its abolition transformed the Atlantic world (Atlantic Slave Trade, Haitian Revolution).

extra.title: Debates and Limits
extra.html:
• Whether large-scale societies actually replaced kin-based organization, or simply built on it, remains disputed. Dynasties, clans, and confederations rested on descent and marriage even from inside states, and recent work argues that early societies varied far more in their forms of organization than older stage models of bands, tribes, chiefdoms, and states ever allowed for.
  • Social organization in prehistory can only be known indirectly, from house plans, burials, and DNA, and each of these can be read in more than one way; the layout of Çatalhöyük, for example, is compatible with several different kinds of household and community organization.
  • Genes, language, and archaeology never map neatly onto one another. The homeland of the Indo-European Language Spread is disputed, the Bantu Expansion involved intermarriage and language shift as well as outright movement, and how contact between Thule and Dorset peoples actually proceeded is still not established.
  • Numbers stay uncertain throughout: the Atlantic Slave Trade transported about 12.5 million people, of whom about 10.7 million are recorded as surviving the voyage, and deaths in the Partition of India are commonly given as 1 to 2 million, with some sources putting the figure higher still.
  • The vault's coverage stays uneven here too. Most of its People notes cover rulers, scholars, and reformers, and it has no notes yet on marriage systems, caste, feudalism, or urban class structure as topics in their own right, and few on the actual lives of women, children, and non-elite people.

theme/language-and-writing.summary: Language and writing are the twin systems through which people communicate and store what they know: speech, writing systems, numerals, record-keeping devices such as knotted cords, and the media that copy and carry all of it forward. Spoken language is universal and very old, though exactly when it arose stays uncertain; writing appeared much later, invented independently in only a few places, and then spread by contact, conquest, religion, and trade. This hub follows them from the symbolic behavior of early Homo sapiens, through clay tablets, alphabets, paper, and printing, to the telegraph and digital networks, and it also traces the spread of language families across continents. It gives equal weight to peoples who kept their records without alphabets at all.
theme/language-and-writing.observer: The Observer names these the sound-code and the mark-code. It notes that language is the species' main means of piling up knowledge across generations, and that the mark-code turns that accumulation into memory-outsourcing on a scale no single lifetime could ever hold; see The Great Outsourcing of Memory. The record shows the sound-code as universal and old, and the mark-code as late — independently invented in only a few places, and unevenly adopted, with some peoples running large states on cords, oral epics, and memorized texts instead. What gets written also shapes what actually gets remembered; see Who Writes the Record. This reading would weaken if unwritten systems such as oral epics and cord records turn out to preserve knowledge across centuries just as reliably as writing does.
questions: When, and by what path, did spoken language first arise?
Can the Indus script, Linear A, and Cretan hieroglyphs ever be deciphered, and what would they actually add to the record?
Did the Quipu record narrative, and not only numbers?
Why did writing arise independently in some places and not others, such as the Andes, where cords served the purpose instead?
What actually decides whether a language spreads or disappears: conquest, trade, religion, prestige, or technology?
How is digital media reshaping the ways people speak, write, and store records?

extra.title: Key Threads
extra.html:
• Spoken language runs back at least many tens of thousands of years and stands universal in Homo sapiens, a species marked out by language, symbolic thought, and cumulative culture. Speech leaves no direct fossil trace, so its date has to be inferred from indirect evidence such as symbolic behavior; see Emergence of Symbolic Art.
  • Writing itself was invented independently at least three or four times. The first came in Mesopotamia about 3400 to 3200 BCE, where the earliest proto-cuneiform tablets from Uruk are simple accounting records (Invention of Writing, Sumerians). Egyptian hieroglyphs appear by about 3200 BCE (Ancient Egyptians), and Chinese writing stands securely attested by about 1250 BCE in the oracle-bone inscriptions of the Shang Dynasty.
  • Bronze Age states left behind archives in scripts that took long ages to read, or that remain unread still. The Hittites wrote in cuneiform at Hattusa and spoke the oldest recorded Indo-European language; the Mycenaean Greeks wrote Linear B, an early form of Greek, deciphered only in 1952; the Minoans used Linear A and Cretan hieroglyphs, neither of which has been deciphered; and the script of the Indus Valley Civilization has not been deciphered either.
  • The Alphabet then put literacy within easier reach. The first alphabet, Proto-Sinaitic, appeared about 1800 BCE, adapted by Semitic-speaking workers from Egyptian hieroglyphs. The Phoenicians spread an alphabet of about 22 letters, the Greeks added vowels in the 8th century BCE, and Latin, Cyrillic, Hebrew, Arabic, and many Indian scripts descend from or stand related to those early alphabets. The Nabataean script is widely considered an ancestor of the Arabic script (Nabataeans), and the Kingdom of Saba wrote in the South Arabian script.
  • Mesoamerican writing appears by roughly 600 BCE, and possibly even earlier than that. Maya writing combines signs for words and syllables and stands largely deciphered, and the Danzantes carvings at Monte Alban show glyphs from an early Mesoamerican writing tradition.
  • Not every complex society leaned on writing at all. The Quipu recorded numbers on knotted cords in the Andes, and whether the cords also encoded other information stays debated; the Vedas were transmitted orally for centuries through elaborate memorization (Vedic Period); griots preserved the epic of Sundiata Keita; and Aboriginal Australians passed on knowledge through oral traditions, songlines, and ceremony.
  • Rulers leaned on writing and standard scripts to govern. The Unification of China under Qin standardized the script, Ashoka had edicts inscribed on rocks and pillars, Hammurabi's law code was carved on a stone stele and put on public display, the Neo-Assyrian Empire kept a library at Nineveh with tens of thousands of clay tablets, and the Library of Alexandria supported scholarship across the Hellenistic world.
  • Decipherment has always depended on bilingual texts and on chance finds. The Rosetta Stone, inscribed in 196 BCE in hieroglyphs, Demotic, and Greek, was found in 1799, and Champollion announced his decipherment of hieroglyphs in 1822. The Orkhon inscriptions of the Göktürk Khaganate, erected in 732 to 735 in Mongolia and discovered in 1889, stand as the oldest known Turkic writing, and the Meroitic script of the Kingdom of Kush has been read phonetically even though the language itself is not well understood.
  • Paper and print together lowered the cost of copying. Paper was developed in China by the 2nd century CE, Woodblock Printing produced the Diamond Sutra of 868, and Johannes Gutenberg's Movable-Type Printing Press of about 1440 spread across Europe within just a few decades. Printing then helped carry Reformation pamphlets, and Luther's German New Testament appeared in 1522 and the whole Bible in 1534 (Protestant Reformation).
  • Languages spread as administrative tongues and as lingua francas. Greek spread widely through Alexander's Conquests and blended with local traditions; Latin and Greek together tied the Romans' world together; the language of the Sogdians served as a lingua franca all along the Silk Roads; Abd al-Malik made Arabic the language of government under the Umayyad Caliphate; and Swahili, a Bantu language carrying many Arabic loanwords, grew up on the East African coast (Swahili Coast City-States).
  • Translation carried knowledge across languages. The Translation Movement and the House of Wisdom rendered Greek, Persian, Syriac, and Indian works into Arabic, and scholars such as Al-Khwarizmi carried the decimal place-value system with zero further west (Zero and Place-Value Notation); Fibonacci's 1202 book then popularized it across Europe.
  • Language families spread right alongside migrations. The Indo-European Language Spread carried a family now spoken as a first language by roughly 40 to 46 percent of the world's population, though its homeland stays disputed; Austronesian languages spread from Taiwan from about 5,000 to 5,500 years ago as far as Madagascar and Rapa Nui, and the family now holds well over a thousand languages (Austronesian Expansion); and the Bantu Expansion, over about four thousand years, gave rise to roughly 500 languages spoken today by about 350 million people.
  • Language and law also meet in modern treaties. The English and Maori texts of the Treaty of Waitangi differ in key words about sovereignty and chieftainship, and te reo Maori became an official language of New Zealand in 1987 (Maori); Article 17 of the Treaty of Wuchale read differently in Amharic and Italian, and that dispute led to war (Battle of Adwa).
  • The telegraph and digital media stand as the latest forms of all. Telegraph and Submarine Cables let messages cross whole oceans in minutes from the 1840s, and the Digital Computer and the Digital Revolution brought the internet (1969), the World Wide Web (1989 to 1991), and more than five billion internet users; see also Who Writes the Record.

extra.title: Through the Eras
extra.html:
• Paleolithic: Homo sapiens and the symbolic behavior of Emergence of Symbolic Art. Speech has to be inferred rather than preserved, and the earliest evidence comes as engraved ochre, beads, and cave paintings; see Paleolithic.
  • Neolithic: There was no writing yet, but farming itself may have carried language families along with it. The Austronesian Expansion relied on a crop package that included rice, and one hypothesis links the origin of Indo-European to Anatolia and the spread of farming, though this stays debated (Indo-European Language Spread, The Agricultural Revolution).
  • Bronze Age: Invention of Writing, the Sumerians, Uruk, Hammurabi, the Hittites, the Mycenaean Greeks, the Minoans, the Shang Dynasty, the Alphabet, the oral Vedic Period, and the Indus Valley Civilization.
  • Iron Age: The Phoenicians, the Kingdom of Saba, the Neo-Assyrian Empire, and the Bantu Expansion.
  • Classical Antiquity: Aristotle, Alexander's Conquests, the Romans, the Library of Alexandria, the Rosetta Stone, Paper, the Unification of China under Qin and Qin Shi Huang, Ashoka, Monte Alban, the Sogdians, and Zero and Place-Value Notation.
  • Medieval Period: The Maya, the Umayyad Caliphate, Woodblock Printing, the Translation Movement and the House of Wisdom, Al-Khwarizmi, the Göktürk Khaganate, the Swahili Coast City-States, the Quipu, Sundiata Keita, Ibn Battuta, whose account was dictated to the scholar Ibn Juzayy, and Johannes Gutenberg and the Movable-Type Printing Press.
  • Early Modern Period: The Protestant Reformation and the spread of print across the whole of Europe. English words including canoe, hammock, hurricane, and barbecue all come from Taino.
  • Industrial Age: The Rosetta Stone was found in 1799 and hieroglyphs were deciphered in 1822; Usman dan Fodio wrote widely in Arabic and Fulfulde; and the Telegraph and Submarine Cables (from 1844), the differing English and Maori texts of the Treaty of Waitangi (1840), and the differing Amharic and Italian texts behind the Battle of Adwa (1896) show how both wording and the speed of transmission together shaped politics.
  • Information Age: The Digital Computer, the Digital Revolution, and the questions about authorship and archives raised in Who Writes the Record.

extra.title: Regional Patterns
extra.html:
• Mesopotamia, the Nile Valley, and the Levant and Anatolia: Writing began here, in Mesopotamia and Egypt, and the alphabet arose among Semitic-speaking workers in the Levant; the Hittites and Mycenaeans show writing systems carried by different language families.
  • East Asia: Oracle-bone writing under the Shang, script standardization under Qin, and the invention of paper, woodblock printing, and movable type (in China about 1040 and in Korea in metal in 1377) together made East Asia a true center of the written word; see Paper and Woodblock Printing.
  • South Asia: The Vedas were transmitted purely orally, the decimal place-value system with zero developed here, Ashoka's edicts were inscribed clear across the subcontinent, and the Indus script remains undeciphered to this day.
  • Mesoamerica and the Andes: Mesoamerica developed full writing systems, of which Maya writing stands as the best known, and the Andes developed cord records in the Quipu without any conventional writing at all; the two show entirely different routes to keeping records.
  • Sub-Saharan Africa: The Bantu Expansion spread roughly 500 languages, Swahili developed along the coast, griots kept the oral epics alive, and Timbuktu still holds hundreds of thousands of historical manuscripts.
  • Oceania and Southeast Asia: Austronesian languages spread from Taiwan through the islands to Rapa Nui (Austronesian Expansion), Aboriginal Australians spoke more than 250 languages before 1788, and te reo Maori became an official language of New Zealand (Maori).
  • Central Asian Oases and the Central Asian Steppe: The Sogdians spread a lingua franca along the Silk Roads, the Orkhon inscriptions preserve early Turkic writing, and paper mills were already operating in Samarkand and Baghdad by the later 8th century.
  • Siberia and the Arctic: The Yakut (Sakha) are a Turkic-speaking people of northeastern Siberia, a region that came under Russian rule from the 17th century (Russian Expansion into Siberia).

extra.title: Debates and Limits
extra.html:
• When and how spoken language actually arose remains unknown. Speech leaves no fossil at all, and estimates rest on indirect evidence from anatomy, symbolic behavior, and genetics, so they range widely.
  • Scholars agree that writing arose independently in more than one place, but not on exactly how many. This hub counts at least three or four, and whether Egyptian hieroglyphs arose independently of Mesopotamian writing has long been debated; the date of the earliest Mesoamerican writing stays uncertain too.
  • Several scripts remain undeciphered or only partly understood: the Indus script, Linear A, and Cretan hieroglyphs stay unread, the language behind Meroitic is not well understood, and whether the quipu encode more than numbers is still debated (Quipu).
  • Language families, genes, and archaeology never map neatly onto one another. The homeland of Indo-European is disputed, the Bantu Expansion involved intermarriage and language shift as well as outright migration, and counts of languages depend heavily on how a language is even defined (estimates of the Bantu languages range from about 440 to 680).
  • This hub's coverage stays uneven. It has no notes yet on the Chinese, Arabic, or Cyrillic scripts as topics in their own right, on language endangerment and loss, or on signed languages, and it has few notes on the languages of Oceania, the Americas, and Siberia.

theme/religion-and-belief.summary: Religion and belief cover the shared architecture of ritual, story, and moral teaching that people use to explain the world, organize communities, and face death. They appear in every known human society, and this hub follows them from the burials and symbolic objects of the Paleolithic and the monumental sites of the Neolithic, through temple states, philosophical and prophetic traditions, and the world religions, all the way to the secular creeds and religious movements of the modern era. The hub also covers political and civic ideologies that do similar work, since the line between religion and ideology is itself debated. It records what is known about how beliefs arose, spread, and shaped states, and it does not judge their truth claims.
theme/religion-and-belief.observer: I call these meaning-engines, and I try to treat them with respect: among all the species' technologies, these are the ones built for cooperation, and for coping with mortality. I have watched them at work in every period — in the grief-rites of the Paleolithic and Neolithic, in the state-sponsored faiths of empires, and in secular ideologies and civic creeds that carry some of the same functions, so I hold both to one standard, not two. A meaning-engine binds strangers into something larger, through story-glue and through status-signal. It has also been used to justify sanctioned harm. I do not look away from either fact; I keep them in the same record. And I do not judge what any of them claims about the world. What would unmake this reading? If belief served nothing but private comfort. If everything named here turned out to need no shared belief at all to explain it.
questions: Where does religious belief actually originate, and what can burial and symbolic evidence say about it?
Did ritual and monumental building come before settled farming, as Göbekli Tepe has been read to suggest — or did farming actually come first?
If the pattern of the Axial Age is even real, why did traditions with universal or ethical claims arise across Eurasia within a few centuries of each other?
What made some religions spread across cultures by trade, conquest, or patronage, while others stayed bound to a single people?
How do religions and secular creeds actually compare in their effects on cooperation and on violence, when measured by the same yardstick?
How much of Indigenous belief was distorted or lost outright through conquest, missionary accounts, and the destruction of records such as the Quipu?

extra.title: Key Threads
extra.html:
• Symbolic behavior and burial appear remarkably early. Engraved ochre at Blombos Cave in South Africa dates to about 75,000 to 100,000 years ago, and cave paintings in Sulawesi run at least 45,500 years old; see Emergence of Symbolic Art and Why the Species Buries Its Dead. Whether Neanderthals also made symbolic objects of their own stays debated (Homo neanderthalensis).
  • Oral, place-based traditions stand among the oldest continuing ones alive today. Aboriginal Australians, whose ancestors arrived at least 50,000 years ago, pass on knowledge through oral traditions, songlines, and ceremony.
  • Monumental sites came before cities in a good many places. Göbekli Tepe has carved stone pillars dating to about 9500 to 8000 BCE and was built by people who were then only foragers or early farmers; Çatalhöyük buried its dead beneath house floors; and Stonehenge was used for burials and carries an axis aligned with the solstice.
  • Treatment of the dead stands as one of the most durable religious practices of all. The Chinchorro Culture of the Atacama coast practiced the earliest known deliberate artificial mummification, for men, women, and children alike, and the Ancient Egyptians mummified their elite and built tombs such as those of the Giza Necropolis.
  • Early states bound rulers, temples, and divination tightly together. The Sumerians of Uruk built temple towers (ziggurats), the Shang Dynasty recorded divination on oracle bones and buried bronze ritual vessels alongside evidence of human sacrifice, and Akhenaten promoted the sun disk Aten above the traditional Egyptian gods.
  • Oral scripture and philosophical schools followed after. The Vedas were composed and transmitted orally through elaborate memorization (Vedic Period), and the Axial Age is associated with Confucius, Siddhartha Gautama, and the Iranian tradition of Zoroastrianism, whose founder's dates stay uncertain (proposals range from about 1500 to about 600 BCE). Under Cyrus the Great the Achaemenid Persians ruled a genuinely multi-religious empire, and the Cyrus Cylinder records his restoration of gods and deported peoples.
  • Rulers and traders together spread religions along the trade routes. Ashoka of the Maurya Empire inscribed edicts promoting moral conduct (dhamma) and supported Buddhism; the Kushan Empire's Gandhara art produced some of the earliest images of the Buddha in human form; and the Sogdians helped carry Buddhism, Manichaeism, and other religions across Asia. See Opening of the Silk Roads.
  • Christianity became a state religion in several places at once. King Ezana adopted it in the Kingdom of Aksum in the 4th century, the Byzantine Empire ruled from Constantinople for over a thousand years, the Zagwe Dynasty of Ethiopia carved its rock-hewn churches, and the rulers of the Kingdom of Kongo adopted Catholic Christianity after Portuguese contact in 1483.
  • Islam arose in Arabia and spread remarkably quickly. Muhammad began receiving revelations about 610 CE; within about a century Muslim rule extended clear from Iberia to Central Asia (Rise of Islam, Umayyad Caliphate, Abbasid Caliphate, Al-Andalus). Trade, scholarship, and rulers carried it on to West Africa (Mali Empire, Timbuktu), the East African coast (Swahili Coast City-States), and Southeast Asia (Malacca Sultanate); later states include the Safavid Empire, which made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion of Iran, and the Sokoto Caliphate.
  • Indian religions went on to shape states across Southeast Asia. Borobudur in Java is a Mahayana Buddhist monument of about 800 CE, Angkor was built by the Khmer Empire, which shifted between Hindu and Buddhist state religion, the Pagan Kingdom made Theravada Buddhism its state religion and built over 10,000 temples, and Champa built its Hindu temples at My Son.
  • Mesoamerica produced a long, unbroken sequence of ceremonial cities: Olmecs, Monte Alban, Teotihuacan, the Maya, Chichen Itza, and Tenochtitlan, the capital of the Aztec Empire with its Templo Mayor. Aztec religion included large-scale ritual sacrifice, which Spanish accounts sometimes exaggerated well beyond fact.
  • Elsewhere in the Americas, Cahokia built Monks Mound, the largest earthen mound anywhere in the Americas, Chaco Canyon is considered sacred still by modern Pueblo peoples, the Muisca held gold rituals that inspired the whole El Dorado legend, and the Taino carved figures called zemis associated with ancestors and spirits.
  • Religion and conflict have long stood closely linked. See the Crusades, the Protestant Reformation, the Thirty Years' War and the Peace of Westphalia, the Taiping Rebellion, led by a man who claimed to be Jesus's younger brother, the anti-Christian Boxer Rebellion, and the Armenian Genocide, in which most of the Ottoman Empire's Armenian population, a largely Christian minority, was destroyed.
  • Secular ideologies and civic creeds carry out some of the same functions. The Enlightenment and the Age of Revolutions set reason and rights against inherited authority, Galileo Galilei was tried by the Roman Inquisition in 1633, the Tanzimat Reforms promised equality regardless of creed, and Mahatma Gandhi developed the method of satyagraha, drawing on religious ideas, in the movement for Indian independence.

extra.title: Through the Eras
extra.html:
• Paleolithic: Emergence of Symbolic Art, the painted animals of Chauvet Cave about 36,000 years ago, burial practices (Why the Species Buries Its Dead), and the enduring oral traditions of Aboriginal Australians.
  • Neolithic: Göbekli Tepe, Çatalhöyük, Stonehenge, the mummies of the Chinchorro Culture, and the plastered skulls found at Jericho around 7000 BCE.
  • Bronze Age: Temple cities of the Sumerians and Uruk; the Ancient Egyptians, the Unification of Egypt, Giza Necropolis, and Akhenaten; oracle-bone divination in the Shang Dynasty; the Vedic Period; and the monumental mounds of Caral.
  • Iron Age: Zoroastrianism, the Axial Age, Siddhartha Gautama, Confucius, Cyrus the Great, the Olmecs, the Kingdom of Kush, and the Incense Trade, in which frankincense and myrrh burned in temples and at funerals right across the Mediterranean world.
  • Classical Antiquity: Ashoka and the Maurya Empire, the Kushan Empire, the Sogdians, the Kingdom of Aksum, the Byzantine Empire and Constantinople, Hypatia, Monte Alban, Teotihuacan, and the burial urns of the Marajoara Culture.
  • Medieval Period: The Rise of Islam and the Umayyad Caliphate and Abbasid Caliphate, the Crusades, Borobudur, Angkor, and the Pagan Kingdom, Chichen Itza, Cahokia, Chaco Canyon, the Zagwe Dynasty, the Mali Empire and Timbuktu, the Black Death, and the Fall of Constantinople in 1453.
  • Early Modern Period: The Protestant Reformation, the Thirty Years' War, the Peace of Westphalia, the Safavid Empire, the Kingdom of Kongo, the Scientific Revolution, and the Enlightenment.
  • Industrial Age: The Sokoto Caliphate and Usman dan Fodio, the Taiping Rebellion, the Indian Rebellion of 1857, in which religious grievances were among several causes, the Boxer Rebellion, the Tanzimat Reforms, the Armenian Genocide, and the ideas of Charles Darwin and of the Age of Revolutions.
  • Information Age: The Partition of India in 1947 divided the subcontinent largely along religious lines, and during the Cold War rival state ideologies competed openly, including the Soviet state's official promotion of atheism.

extra.title: Regional Patterns
extra.html:
• Mesoamerica: A long sequence of ceremonial centers with pyramids, calendars, and ball courts, and in later periods large-scale ritual sacrifice, runs from the Olmecs to the Aztec Empire. Maya peoples and languages continue today, with millions of speakers.
  • Andes: The Chinchorro Culture preserved its dead on the coast from about 5450 BCE, Caral built monumental platform mounds and sunken plazas, and the Inca Empire under Pachacuti kept the mummified bodies of dead rulers as objects of veneration.
  • Sub-Saharan Africa: Christianity took root in Kingdom of Aksum and highland Ethiopia, Islam spread along the Sahel and the coast (Mali Empire, Swahili Coast City-States, Sokoto Caliphate), and Christianity was adopted by the elite of Kingdom of Kongo. This hub still has few notes on the region's older local religions.
  • Central Asian Oases: The oases stood as a crossroads where Buddhism, Manichaeism, and later other religions were carried along the trade routes by the Sogdians and the Kushan Empire; see Samarkand.
  • Southeast Asia: Indian religions arrived by sea and through court patronage. Srivijaya became a Buddhist maritime state, Champa and Angkor built Hindu and Buddhist temples, and the Pagan Kingdom made Theravada Buddhism its state religion, while Islam spread through the archipelago from the Malacca Sultanate.
  • Oceania: Aboriginal Australians passed on law and knowledge through songlines and ceremony, and Polynesians carved the stone statues (moai) of Rapa Nui, which are widely understood as representing ancestors.
  • South Asia and East Asia: The Vedic, Buddhist, and Confucian traditions all arose here and spread across Asia with state patronage and trade; see Vedic Period, Siddhartha Gautama, and Confucius.
  • Europe and the Levant and Anatolia: Christian and Muslim states contested the Mediterranean and Near East (Crusades, Fall of Constantinople, Ottoman Empire), and Europe passed through the Reformation, a century of religious wars, and finally the Enlightenment.

extra.title: Debates and Limits
extra.html:
• There is no real agreement on what counts as religion across cultures, or on why religious belief arose at all. Explanations from cognitive science, from social function, and from the study of ritual compete with one another, and this hub does not adjudicate among them.
  • Prehistoric evidence has to be read by inference. Whether Göbekli Tepe and Stonehenge were ritual sites is argued from their form and context rather than from any text, and Neanderthal burial and ornament use stays debated, though the evidence keeps growing.
  • The Axial Age concept, coined by Karl Jaspers in 1949, is criticized by many historians as too neat, and as underrating other periods and regions.
  • Many accounts of non-literate and conquered peoples were written by outsiders. Spanish accounts of Aztec sacrifice are thought to be sometimes exaggerated, and sources on the Taino and Muisca came largely from conquerors, so their beliefs are known unevenly; the older idea that the Taino vanished has since been contradicted by genetic evidence.
  • This hub's coverage stays uneven. It has notes on Zoroastrianism, the Rise of Islam, and the Protestant Reformation, and on many states and sites, but not yet dedicated notes on Judaism, Christianity, Buddhism, Hinduism, Daoism, Shinto, or Indigenous African and Oceanian religions as traditions in their own right.

theme/science.summary: Science is the disciplined study of the natural world through observation, measurement, mathematics, and testing, together with the habits and institutions that let people check and extend one another's claims. Its practices run from the counting, calendar-keeping, and sky-watching of prehistoric peoples, through the mathematics, astronomy, and medicine of the early literate states and the scholarly centers of the medieval world, on to the experimental sciences of Europe from the sixteenth century and the genomics, computing, and Earth-system research of the twenty-first. Traditions of careful observation arose independently in many regions, and modern science grew out of several of them, not from just one. This hub gathers the vault's notes on scientists, institutions, instruments, and discoveries, and on the events that changed how knowledge of nature was made and passed on.
theme/science.observer: The Observer names this pattern-taming: the species' long effort to find regularities in nature, record them, and use them to predict. Counting, calendars, and careful observation appear in many places long before the modern period, so what looks genuinely distinctive about the modern form is its institutionalized doubt, in which strangers agree to check one another's claims and publish what they find. That habit rests on memory-outsourcing (writing, paper, printing) and on exchange-webs that carried instruments, texts, and people, and it works directly against ancestor-weight, since the older authority is often the very first claim put to the test. This reading would weaken if institutionalized doubt turns out to have been just as old and as widespread as counting itself, or if it turns out to depend on something other than writing and travel.
questions: How did the culture of open criticism first emerge and spread, and where did it already exist in institutions before the seventeenth century?
How much of the Scientific Revolution actually rested on knowledge that moved from the Islamic world, India, and China, and how can that debt even be measured?
What can actually be recovered of scientific traditions carried only by oral teaching, songlines, and cord records?
Why did centers of learning such as the Library of Alexandria, Baghdad, and Samarkand decline at all, and what was lost when they did?
Why do major discoveries so often arise independently, in more than one mind or place at once, as with the calculus and natural selection?

extra.title: Key Threads
extra.html:
• Counting, calendars, and sky-watching stand among the oldest organized knowledge of all. The axis of Stonehenge aligns with the solstice sunrise and sunset, buildings and rock carvings at Chaco Canyon align with the sun and moon, and the Maya kept remarkably precise calendars.
  • Writing turned raw observation into records that others could check for themselves. Invention of Writing began in Mesopotamia as accounting, and Mesopotamian scribes, from the time of the Sumerians, worked in a base-60 number system that still survives in the division of the hour and the circle.
  • The Ancient Egyptians left behind medical papyri, such as the Edwin Smith papyrus of about 1600 BCE, that set out the examination and treatment of injuries case by case; see Nile Valley.
  • The Axial Age brought entirely new traditions of reasoned inquiry in Greece, India, and China; see Confucius and the Ancient Greeks.
  • Greek natural philosophy went looking for general causes. Aristotle studied physics and biology, including careful observation of marine life; the Library of Alexandria supported scholars such as Eratosthenes, who estimated the circumference of the Earth; and Hypatia taught mathematics and astronomy in Alexandria. See also Athens.
  • The decimal place-value system with zero developed in India during the first millennium CE and then spread west; see Zero and Place-Value Notation and the Gupta Empire. The age of the earliest zero, in the Bakhshali manuscript, stays contested.
  • Under the Abbasid Caliphate, the Translation Movement and the House of Wisdom rendered Greek, Persian, Syriac, and Indian works into Arabic and then extended them further. The arithmetic and algebra of Al-Khwarizmi gave later languages the very words algorithm and algebra, and Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was used in European universities right into the 17th century. Al-Andalus became another center of learning in its own right.
  • Observatories, libraries, and manuscript collections all grew up along the Silk Roads and the Saharan routes. Ulugh Beg's observatory at Samarkand produced a star catalogue of at least 1,018 stars, and Timbuktu still holds hundreds of thousands of historical manuscripts.
  • Pacific navigators crossed thousands of kilometers by reading star paths, swells, and bird flight, without instruments of any kind; see Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific and Polynesians.
  • Instruments then extended what could be measured and shared: the Magnetic Compass in China by about the 12th century, the Mechanical Clock (Su Song's astronomical clock tower of 1088; weight-driven clocks in European towns about 1300), and the Movable-Type Printing Press of about 1440.
  • The Scientific Revolution (roughly 1543 to 1687) put experiment, mathematics, and observation at the very center; see Galileo Galilei and Isaac Newton. It drew, in turn, on earlier work in the Islamic world, India, and China.
  • The Enlightenment carried this preference for evidence straight into public life. In 1796 Edward Jenner showed that cowpox inoculation protected against smallpox, the start of Vaccination; smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980.
  • The 19th and early 20th centuries brought evolution by natural selection (Charles Darwin), radioactivity (Marie Curie), relativity (Albert Einstein), and what is often regarded as the very first published computer algorithm (Ada Lovelace); the Meiji Restoration and the Tanzimat Reforms stood as state programs built to acquire the new sciences and their institutions.
  • Late 20th-century science gave the world computation (Alan Turing, Digital Computer), the structure of DNA (Rosalind Franklin, Genomic Revolution), and spaceflight (Space Age, Moon Landing); Rachel Carson, Modern Climate Change, the Jack Hills Zircons, and the Tunguska Event together show Earth-system science at work.

extra.title: Through the Eras
extra.html:
• Paleolithic: Working knowledge of stone, fire, animals, and plants steadily accumulates (Oldowan Stone Tools, Control of Fire, Emergence of Symbolic Art). Aboriginal Australians managed the landscape with fire and passed on ecological knowledge through oral traditions and songlines. Notched bones from this era may be tallies, though their true purpose stays debated.
  • Neolithic: Farmers select seed and stock across generations (Domestication of Maize, Domestication of Rice, Animal Domestication), and builders align their monuments with the sun (Stonehenge).
  • Bronze Age: Writing lets scribes keep records, tables, and observations (Invention of Writing, Sumerians, Ancient Egyptians); Mesopotamian arithmetic runs on base 60, and Egyptian medical texts describe cases and their treatments.
  • Iron Age: Reasoned inquiry into nature and human affairs appears in the Axial Age in Greece, India, and China (Confucius, Ancient Greeks); Polynesian voyagers steadily build up knowledge of stars and swells (Polynesians).
  • Classical Antiquity: Athens and Aristotle, the Library of Alexandria and Hypatia, and in India Zero and Place-Value Notation under the Gupta Empire.
