The Han Dynasty kept careful astronomical records, and its scholar Zhang Heng built a seismoscope in 132 CE. The Opening of the Silk Roads moved ideas right alongside goods.
  • Medieval Period: The Translation Movement and the House of Wisdom, Al-Khwarizmi, Ibn Sina, and Al-Andalus; the Song Dynasty's Magnetic Compass and Gunpowder; the Maya calendar and astronomy; Chaco Canyon; Ulugh Beg and the Timurid Empire; Timbuktu; Ibn Khaldun's theory of how states rise and fall; the Mechanical Clock; the Renaissance.
  • Early Modern Period: The Scientific Revolution (Galileo Galilei, Isaac Newton), the Enlightenment, and Vaccination (1796).
  • Industrial Age: The Industrial Revolution created a whole new demand for measurement and engineering. Charles Darwin, Ada Lovelace, Marie Curie, Albert Einstein, Antibiotics, Nuclear Fission, and the Electrical Power Grid all belong here, as do state modernization programs such as the Meiji Restoration and Tanzimat Reforms.
  • Information Age: Alan Turing and the Digital Computer, Rosalind Franklin and the Genomic Revolution, the Space Age and Moon Landing, Rachel Carson and Modern Climate Change, the Green Revolution, and the COVID-19 Pandemic, in which mRNA vaccines were developed and authorized within about a year.

extra.title: Regional Patterns
extra.html:
• Mesopotamia and the Nile Valley: The earliest written mathematics, astronomy, and medicine run back to temple and palace administration; see Sumerians and Ancient Egyptians.
  • South Asia and the Islamic world: Place-value notation with zero arose in India and was carried west by scholars of the Abbasid Caliphate and Al-Andalus; Latin translations of Arabic texts fed European scholarship in the 12th century.
  • East Asia: Paper, printing, the compass, and gunpowder were all documented first in China, and the Song Dynasty stood as a center of technical and commercial innovation.
  • Central Asia: The oases were a crossroads for learning. Ibn Sina was born near Bukhara, Ulugh Beg built his observatory at Samarkand, and the Timurid Empire patronized it; see Central Asian Oases.
  • Oceania: Polynesian voyagers navigated without instruments (Polynesians), the Kuk Early Agricultural Site preserves at least 7,000 years of wetland gardening, and the Jack Hills Zircons in Western Australia hold the oldest known pieces of Earth's crust, about 4.4 billion years old.
  • Mesoamerica and the Andes: The Maya kept precise calendars and used the concept of zero, and the Andean Quipu recorded numbers in a decimal system on knotted cords.
  • Sub-Saharan Africa: Scholarship in Timbuktu and much of the fossil evidence for human origins (Divergence of the Hominin Lineage, Origin of Homo sapiens) come from this region.
  • Siberia and the Arctic: The Tunguska Event of 1908 was first studied on site by an expedition in 1927, and Arctic peoples such as the Inuit built up detailed knowledge of ice, weather, and animal behavior for survival (Inuit and the Thule Expansion).

extra.title: Debates and Limits
extra.html:
• Whether star-lore, navigation, and Indigenous ecological knowledge deserve the name science, or only the experimental and mathematical tradition of recent centuries does, stays disputed. This hub uses a broad definition and treats the narrower one as a later development.
  • Historians debate whether the Scientific Revolution was really a single revolution at all, and how much it actually owed to earlier work in the Islamic world, India, and China. The exact nature of the House of Wisdom is debated too, and the Library of Alexandria declined over centuries rather than in any one fire.
  • Credit stays contested in many cases: the earliest zero (Zero and Place-Value Notation), the calculus, which Isaac Newton developed independently of Leibniz, natural selection, which Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace reached quite separately, the use of Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data in the double-helix model, and Lise Meitner's exclusion from the 1944 Nobel Prize for Nuclear Fission.
  • Science carried only by oral teaching, songlines, and cord records left behind few written texts, so it is all too easy to undercount.
  • This hub's science notes lean toward Europe, the Islamic world, and named individuals. It has few notes on scientists in Africa south of the Sahara, Oceania, the Andes, and Mesoamerica, and none yet on Indian astronomy or Chinese mathematics as topics in their own right.

theme/technology.summary: Technology is the making and use of tools, techniques, and systems built to extend what people can do. It is cumulative by nature: each generation builds on the tools of the last, and the record runs from the first chipped stones, at least 2.6 million years ago, through fire, pottery, farming, metals, writing, and printing, on to engines, electric grids, and digital networks. This hub covers materials, energy, transport, information, food, medicine, and the built environment, and it links the vault's technology notes to the events, places, and peoples through which each technique arose and spread. Many techniques arose independently in more than one region, and others crossed whole continents within a few centuries.
theme/technology.observer: The Observer names this the tool-lineage: an inheritance in which each tool makes the next one possible. The lineage branches rather than running in any single line, and it sometimes breaks outright when a technique dies with its makers, yet similar solutions such as farming and writing appear in unconnected branches, which suggests that some steps are shaped by shared needs and materials, and not only by chance. Memory-outsourcing made the lineage far easier to carry across generations, and ancestor-weight can keep a working technique in use long after real alternatives exist. The lineage is now old enough that no single person understands the whole of it anymore. The Observer would revise this reading if apparent independent origins prove to be diffusion after all, or if the loss of techniques turns out to be far more common than the record shows.
questions: Do technologies actually follow a predictable order, or is the whole sequence contingent?
Why did some techniques, such as farming and writing, arise independently in several regions at once, while others, such as wheeled transport, were never used in the Americas before contact?
How much perishable technology — wood, cord, cloth, basketry — is simply missing from the record, and how can its true scale even be estimated?
Where did the pace of change actually shift decisively: with fire, farming, writing, the steam engine, or the Great Acceleration?

How were techniques actually carried between cultures — by traders, craftspeople, captives, missionaries, and armies — and which traditional stories, such as papermaking at Battle of Talas, survive real scrutiny?

extra.title: Key Threads
extra.html:
• Stone tools begin at least 2.6 million years ago in Africa; see Oldowan Stone Tools and Homo habilis, and, later still, the handaxes made by Homo erectus.
  • Control of Fire stands as an early energy technology in its own right. Evidence at Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa dates to about one million years ago, habitual use is well established by about 400,000 years ago, and cooked food may well have supported larger brains.
  • Pottery appears in East Asia at least 20,000 years ago, well before farming ever did; see Jomon Culture.
  • Farming and herding arose independently in several regions at once, and each brought new techniques with it: see The Agricultural Revolution, Animal Domestication, Domestication of Rice in the Yangtze region, Domestication of Maize in Mexico, and the drained wetland gardens of the Kuk Early Agricultural Site in New Guinea.
  • Wheeled vehicles appear around 3500 to 3000 BCE (The Wheel). Bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, was first widely produced in the Near East around 3300 BCE, and tin itself had to be traded over long distances (Bronze Metallurgy). On the steppe, the Botai Culture managed horses and the Sintashta Culture built the earliest known spoke-wheeled chariots.
  • Recording systems arose in several places quite independently. Invention of Writing happened independently at least three or four times, first in Mesopotamia about 3400 to 3200 BCE; the Alphabet (Proto-Sinaitic, about 1800 BCE) gave rise to most alphabets still in use today; and in the Andes knotted cords served as records (Quipu, with possible early relatives at Caral).
  • Iron smelting began on a limited scale in Anatolia in the early 2nd millennium BCE and then spread widely from about 1200 BCE (Iron Smelting). Ironworking in Africa, including at Meroe in the Kingdom of Kush and among Bantu-speaking peoples (Bantu Expansion), remains a case where independent invention is debated.
  • Paper was developed in China somewhere between about the 2nd century BCE and the 2nd century CE (Paper, Han Dynasty). Woodblock Printing produced the Diamond Sutra of 868, the oldest dated printed book, and movable type appeared in China about 1040 and in Korea (metal type) in 1377, well before Johannes Gutenberg's Movable-Type Printing Press in Mainz about 1440.
  • Under the Song Dynasty gunpowder became a military technology and the compass came into use for navigation at sea; see Gunpowder and Magnetic Compass. Su Song built an astronomical clock tower in 1088, and weight-driven mechanical clocks with escapements appeared in European towns about 1300 (Mechanical Clock).
  • Ocean and polar travel demanded their own techniques: Polynesians settled the remote Pacific in double-hulled canoes using non-instrument navigation (Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific); the Thule ancestors of the Inuit used dog sleds, skin boats, and toggling harpoons (Inuit and the Thule Expansion); and the Norse crossed the North Atlantic, reaching L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland by 1021.
  • Large-scale landscape engineering appears in many regions at once: the reservoirs and canals of Angkor and the Khmer Empire, the earthworks and enriched soils of Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths (see Upano Valley Settlements and Xingu Garden Cities), the road system of the Inca Empire, roughly 30,000 to 40,000 kilometers long, and the dry-stone walls of Great Zimbabwe.
  • Steam power (Steam Engine: Newcomen 1712, Watt's separate condenser patented 1769) drove the Industrial Revolution and made Railways possible in turn; the Telegraph and Submarine Cables then carried messages across oceans, and works such as the Suez Canal (1869) and the Trans-Siberian Railway (1891 to 1916) followed close behind.
  • The Electrical Power Grid began with the first commercial power station in 1882. Nuclear Fission, discovered in 1938, led on to reactors and weapons alike (Nuclear Age). Vaccination (1796), Antibiotics (1928), and the Green Revolution together changed health and food supply.
  • The Digital Computer (ENIAC, 1945) then shrank with the transistor (1947) and the integrated circuit (about 1958). The Digital Revolution brought the internet (1969), the World Wide Web (1991), and smartphones (about 2007), and the Space Age began with Sputnik in 1957; see Alan Turing.

extra.title: Through the Eras
extra.html:
• Paleolithic: Oldowan Stone Tools, Control of Fire, the handaxes of Homo erectus, Pottery about 20,000 years ago, open-sea crossings all the way to Sahul at least 50,000 years ago (Peopling of Sahul), and the wooden hut foundations, leather, and rope preserved at Monte Verde.
  • Neolithic: Farming and herding (The Agricultural Revolution, Animal Domestication, Domestication of Rice, Domestication of Maize), stone building at Jericho, where a wall and tower date to roughly 8000 BCE, pottery-making hunter-gatherers (Jomon Culture), and artificial mummification from about 5050 BCE (Chinchorro Culture).
  • Bronze Age: The Wheel, Bronze Metallurgy, Invention of Writing, the Alphabet, and cities (The Urban Revolution); planned streets, drainage, and standard weights in the Indus Valley Civilization; spoke-wheeled chariots (Sintashta Culture); large stone construction at Giza Necropolis and platform mounds at Caral.
  • Iron Age: Iron Smelting, ironworking at Meroe in the Kingdom of Kush, farming and ironworking carried by the Bantu Expansion, and Pacific voyaging by the Polynesians.
  • Classical Antiquity: Paper under the Han Dynasty; the standardization of writing, weights, measures, and currency in the Unification of China under Qin; roads, aqueducts, and concrete in the Romans' empire; Zero and Place-Value Notation in India; and, from about 500 BCE, the settlement networks of Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths and the Upano Valley Settlements.
  • Medieval Period: Woodblock Printing, Gunpowder, the Magnetic Compass, the Mechanical Clock, the Quipu, and the Movable-Type Printing Press; water works at Angkor; stone building at Great Zimbabwe; Norse and Thule seafaring (Norse, Inuit and the Thule Expansion); and the Inca royal estate at Machu Picchu.
  • Early Modern Period: The first commercially successful Steam Engine (1712); ocean routes opened by ships armed with cannon (Portuguese Sea Route to India); crops and animals crossing the Atlantic (Columbian Exchange); instruments and print in the Scientific Revolution; and Vaccination in 1796.
  • Industrial Age: The Industrial Revolution, Railways (1825), the Telegraph and Submarine Cables (1844), the Electrical Power Grid (1882), the Trans-Siberian Railway, the Suez Canal, Antibiotics (1928), and Nuclear Fission (1938). States such as Egypt under Muhammad Ali of Egypt, Japan in the Meiji Restoration, and Ethiopia under Menelik II sought to acquire industrial and military technology.
  • Information Age: The Digital Computer, the Digital Revolution, the Nuclear Age, the Green Revolution, the Space Age and Moon Landing, the Genomic Revolution (CRISPR gene editing, 2012), and the Great Acceleration, in which energy and fertilizer use have risen steeply since about 1950.

extra.title: Regional Patterns
extra.html:
• East Asia: Pottery, paper, printing, gunpowder, and the compass were all documented first here. Several reached the west along the Silk Roads and through the Mongol Empire; see Opening of the Silk Roads.
  • Sub-Saharan Africa: The earliest known stone tools come from here (Oldowan Stone Tools), as does much of the debate over African ironworking; the Bantu Expansion carried farming and iron right across the continent, and Great Zimbabwe shows dry-stone building at real scale.
  • Andes: The Quipu recorded numbers on knotted cords, the Chinchorro Culture practiced the earliest known deliberate artificial mummification, and the Inca Empire built a road system running tens of thousands of kilometers. The wheel was not used for transport in the Americas before contact (The Wheel).
  • Mesoamerica: Maize was domesticated here, and cooking it with lime (nixtamalization) makes its nutrients available (Domestication of Maize). Tenochtitlan was fed in part by chinampas, and the Maya developed a full writing system.
  • Oceania: People crossed open sea to Sahul at least 50,000 years ago (Peopling of Sahul), cultivated drained wetlands in New Guinea (Kuk Early Agricultural Site), and later settled the far Pacific (Polynesians).
  • Central Asian Steppe: Horse management at Botai Culture sites and spoke-wheeled chariots at Sintashta Culture settlements both come from the steppe.
  • Siberia and the Arctic: Inuit and the Thule Expansion shows cold-climate technology (dog sleds, skin boats, toggling harpoons), Yakut (Sakha) herders adapted horses and cattle to one of the coldest inhabited regions on Earth, and the Trans-Siberian Railway later crossed the region.
  • Southeast Asia and the Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands: Both regions show large-scale water and soil engineering, from the reservoirs of Angkor to the dark earths and earthworks of Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths.

extra.title: Debates and Limits
extra.html:
• Independent invention versus diffusion stays disputed in many cases. Writing arose independently at least three or four times, but scholars are divided on whether African ironworking was independent of the Near East, and the spread of papermaking and printing across Eurasia can only be traced in part.
  • Single-inventor stories usually compress much longer processes than they let on. Movable type was used in China and Korea before Gutenberg, paper fragments predate the traditional date credited to Cai Lun, and the Steam Engine of Newcomen preceded Watt's improvements.
  • The record stays biased toward durable materials. Wood, cord, cloth, and basketry rarely survive at all, Spanish colonial authorities banned or destroyed many quipus (Quipu), and earlier stone tools than the Oldowan, such as reports from Lomekwi in Kenya of about 3.3 million years ago, remain under study.
  • Whether technologies drive social change, or are themselves shaped by it, stays contested, and this hub does not try to settle it.
  • This hub's coverage stays uneven. It has no notes yet on optics, sanitation, aviation, semiconductors, or GPS as technologies in their own right, and few on non-Western techniques such as crucible steel, porcelain, qanats, chinampas, or outrigger canoes.

theme/trade-and-economy.summary: Trade and economy cover the production, exchange, and taxation of goods, labor, and money, and the institutions built to organize them: markets, credit, coinage, companies, tribute, and forced labor. This hub traces exchange from the long-distance movement of stone and shells in prehistory, through Bronze Age metal trade, the Silk Road, Indian Ocean, and trans-Saharan networks, and the global commerce created after 1492, on to the industrial production and digital economy of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Trade carried ideas, religions, crops, and diseases right alongside goods, and it also included the coerced trade in people. This hub gathers the vault's notes on routes, trading states, commodities, and economic systems.
theme/trade-and-economy.observer: The Observer names these exchange-webs and notes that they have no owner and no center. Trade repeatedly turns strangers into partners, and transmits pathogens just as readily as products. The record suggests that exchange-webs rest on trust that has to be built, through shared accounts, coinage, law, and other story-glue, and that they sit right beside coercive extraction — tribute, forced labor, and the trade in people — which the Observer records in the same ledger, rather than in a separate one (see Frontiers of Extraction). Networks that carried goods also carried ideas, religions, crops, and diseases, so the Observer refuses to treat them as merely economic. This reading would weaken if long-distance trade proves to have been driven mainly by states and elites, with little of the decentralized quality the term implies.
questions: How did early markets and money actually emerge?
How much long-distance exchange before writing can actually be reconstructed from materials alone, and how reliable are those inferences?
Why did some exchange routes last for centuries — the Silk Roads, the Indian Ocean, the trans-Saharan routes — while others collapsed outright, as in the Bronze Age Collapse?
How did trade, tribute, and coercion actually interact in empires such as the Aztec Empire, the Inca Empire, the Romans, and the Qing Dynasty?
Why did sustained growth in output per person begin exactly when and where it did?
How far did trade itself spread disease, from the Black Death to the 1918 Influenza Pandemic and the COVID-19 Pandemic, and how did societies actually respond?

extra.title: Key Threads
extra.html:
• Long-distance exchange of stone and shells runs back tens of thousands of years. The Lapita Culture moved obsidian and other goods over long distances across the western Pacific, and the hunter-gatherer-fishers of Poverty Point in Louisiana brought in stone and other materials from hundreds of kilometers away, between about 1700 and 1100 BCE.
  • Farming supported denser populations and permanent settlement (The Agricultural Revolution), and the first cities followed close behind (The Urban Revolution, Uruk, Sumerians). Invention of Writing began as a way to record goods and obligations, and the earliest tablets from Uruk stand as accounting records. Bronze Metallurgy made trade essential, since tin was scarce and had to be carried over long distances from places such as Afghanistan and later Cornwall.
  • Bronze Age networks tied together the eastern Mediterranean, Anatolia, Egypt, and the Indus. The Indus Valley Civilization traded with Mesopotamia and made goods to standard weights, the Minoans traded across the eastern Mediterranean, and Hatshepsut sponsored a trading expedition to Punt. The Bronze Age Collapse around 1200 BCE ended the palace economies outright, and the breakdown of trade networks stands among the proposed causes.
  • Caravan and sea traders grew rich simply as middlemen. The Incense Trade carried frankincense and myrrh from southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa by camel caravan; the Kingdom of Saba and the Nabataeans profited from taxing and guiding the caravans; and the Phoenicians of the Levant coast founded colonies, including Carthage, and spread a simple alphabet along with their trade.
  • The Opening of the Silk Roads from the second century BCE linked East Asia, South Asia, Central Asia, and the Mediterranean together. Goods included silk, horses, glass, spices, and paper, and disease traveled the same routes too (Black Death). The Han Dynasty paid the Xiongnu annual gifts, the Kushan Empire connected Rome, Parthia, India, and Han China commercially, and the Sogdians became the leading Silk Road merchants, acting as caravan leaders, interpreters, and bankers all at once.
  • Large states built their economies around roads, taxation, and records. The Romans were tied together by Latin, Greek, and trade, Augustus reorganized the army, provinces, and taxation, the Kingdom of Aksum controlled Red Sea trade between Rome, Arabia, and India and minted its own coins, and the Persepolis tablets of the Achaemenid Persians record rations and administration (Persepolis).
  • The Indian Ocean Trade Network rode the monsoon winds and was busiest from about the 8th to the 15th century, carrying spices, cotton textiles, ivory, gold, and Chinese porcelain. The Swahili Coast City-States, such as Kilwa, which minted its own coins, grew rich from it directly; Srivijaya controlled shipping through the Strait of Malacca; the Chola Dynasty traded with China and Southeast Asia; and the Malacca Sultanate became the leading port of Southeast Asia in the 15th century, before the Portuguese took it in 1511 (Portuguese Sea Route to India).
  • Trans-Saharan trade in gold, salt, and ivory sustained the Ghana Empire, the Mali Empire, and the Songhai Empire in turn. Mansa Musa's pilgrimage in 1324 reportedly disrupted the gold market in Cairo, and Timbuktu became a real hub of trade and scholarship. Farther south, Great Zimbabwe traded gold and ivory with the Swahili coast, and the Kingdom of Mapungubwe received glass beads and Chinese celadon through East African harbors.
  • East Asia stood as a commercial center in its own right. The Tang Dynasty's capital Chang'an held about a million people; the Song Dynasty issued some of the world's first government paper money; American silver, arriving through the Manila trade, became a major part of the Ming Dynasty economy; and the Tokugawa Shogunate limited foreign trade to only Dutch and Chinese merchants at Nagasaki.
  • Exchange and tribute in the pre-Columbian Americas took forms unlike anything in Eurasia. Caral combined coastal fishing with inland farming, Teotihuacan had wide trade and political links, Chaco Canyon was a ceremonial and trade center with roads radiating out from it, the Aztec Empire collected tribute from conquered city-states, and the Inca Empire exacted labor service (mit'a) rather than money taxes and kept its records on Quipu.
  • After 1492 trade turned genuinely global. The Columbian Exchange moved plants, animals, people, and diseases between the hemispheres; the Manila Galleon Trade (1565 to 1815) carried Chinese goods to the Americas and American silver to Asia, much of it from Potosi, where the Spanish organized labor through the mita; and the Dutch East India Company, chartered in 1602, stood among the first companies to issue tradable shares, and had powers to wage war and build forts of its own.
  • Coerced labor underpinned much of the Atlantic economy. The Atlantic Slave Trade forcibly transported about 12.5 million Africans to the Americas, the Sugar Plantation Complex drove much of that demand, the Haitian Revolution arose in Saint-Domingue, the largest sugar producer in the world in the late 18th century, and the Abolition of Slavery followed between 1807 and 1888.
  • The Industrial Revolution began in Britain about 1760 with the shift to machine production driven by coal and steam, and economic output per person began, for the first time in history, to rise steadily. The Steam Engine, Railways, the Telegraph and Submarine Cables, the Electrical Power Grid, and the Suez Canal, which cut the voyage between Europe and India by thousands of kilometers, together reshaped trade across the 19th century.
  • Modern economies were shaped just as much by empire as by state policy. The Opium Wars opened China to Western commerce on unequal terms, the Scramble for Africa and the Congo Free State built forced-labor extraction, and after 1950 the Great Acceleration raised output and energy use steeply. Chinese Reform and Opening (from December 1978) brought market reforms and decades of rapid growth, the Digital Revolution spread computing and networks, and the COVID-19 Pandemic disrupted supply chains right across the world.

extra.title: Through the Eras
extra.html:
• Paleolithic: Stone, shell, and pigment moved between hunter-gatherer groups over long distances, but the evidence stays fragmentary, and this hub has no dedicated note yet on Paleolithic exchange; see Paleolithic.
  • Neolithic: Farming and herding (The Agricultural Revolution, Animal Domestication) created storable surpluses and traction animals, and Pottery let food and liquids be stored and carried.
  • Bronze Age: The Urban Revolution, Uruk, Sumerians, Invention of Writing, Bronze Metallurgy, The Wheel, the Indus Valley Civilization, the Minoans, the Hittites, Hatshepsut's expedition to Punt, Caral, Poverty Point, the Lapita Culture, and the Bronze Age Collapse.
  • Iron Age: The Incense Trade, the Kingdom of Saba, the Phoenicians, Carthage, the Scythians, Samarkand, the Olmecs, the Achaemenid Persians, and Iron Smelting.
  • Classical Antiquity: The Opening of the Silk Roads, the Han Dynasty and Xiongnu, the Romans and Augustus, the Nabataeans, the Kushan Empire, the Sogdians, the Kingdom of Aksum, Teotihuacan, the Maurya Empire, and Zero and Place-Value Notation, which made calculation easier.
  • Medieval Period: The Indian Ocean Trade Network, the Swahili Coast City-States, Srivijaya, the Abbasid Caliphate, the Tang Dynasty and Song Dynasty, the Ghana Empire, Mali Empire, and Timbuktu, Great Zimbabwe, the Kingdom of Mapungubwe, Chaco Canyon, Cahokia, the Mongol Empire, whose relay postal system sped communication across Eurasia, the Norse, who traded in eastern Europe for silver from the Islamic world, the Malacca Sultanate, Zheng He, Ibn Battuta, and the Black Death.
  • Early Modern Period: The Columbian Exchange, the Portuguese Sea Route to India, the Manila Galleon Trade, Potosi, the Dutch East India Company, the Atlantic Slave Trade, the Sugar Plantation Complex, the Ming Dynasty, the Mughal Empire, which by 1700 ruled about 100 million people and made India one of the world's largest economies, the Tokugawa Shogunate, and the Russian Expansion into Siberia, driven by the fur trade.
  • Industrial Age: The Industrial Revolution, Railways, the Telegraph and Submarine Cables, the Electrical Power Grid, the Suez Canal, the Trans-Siberian Railway, the Opium Wars, the British Raj, the Scramble for Africa, the Congo Free State, the Abolition of Slavery, and the Bengal Famine of 1943, which Amartya Sen analyzed as an entitlement failure: food supply did not fall sharply, but economic pressures kept some groups from buying it.
  • Information Age: Decolonization, the Green Revolution, the Great Acceleration, the Digital Revolution, Chinese Reform and Opening, and the COVID-19 Pandemic.

extra.title: Regional Patterns
extra.html:
• Sub-Saharan Africa: Gold, salt, and ivory sustained the Sahelian empires and Swahili city-states, and the interior states of Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe reached the Indian Ocean; from the 16th century the Kingdom of Kongo was drawn into the Atlantic slave trade (Atlantic Slave Trade), and between 1885 and 1908 the Congo Free State extracted rubber and ivory through forced labor.
  • Central Asian Oases and the Central Asian Steppe: The Sogdians of the oases stood as the leading Silk Road merchants, and steppe powers such as the Xiongnu and the Mongol Empire taxed, protected, and raided the routes in turn; see Samarkand.
  • Southeast Asia: Control of the straits made Srivijaya and the Malacca Sultanate rich, Champa traded across the South China Sea, and later the Manila Galleon Trade and the Dutch East India Company (which founded Batavia in 1619) tied the region tightly to European and American markets.
  • Andes: Caral linked coast and highland, the Inca Empire ran a state economy on labor service and recorded goods on Quipu, and after the Spanish conquest the silver of Potosi, worked under a forced-labor draft adapted from an Inca system, supplied world trade.
  • Mesoamerica: Domestication of Maize made a staple crop for the whole of the Americas, Teotihuacan had wide trade links, and the Aztec Empire collected tribute from conquered city-states for Tenochtitlan.
  • Oceania: The Lapita Culture and later the Polynesians moved goods and people across thousands of kilometers of open sea, and the Treaty of Waitangi of 1840 was followed by conflict over land and authority.
  • Siberia and the Arctic: European demand for furs drove the Russian Expansion into Siberia between 1582 and 1639, and the Yakut (Sakha) paid yasak, a fur tribute, until 1917; the Trans-Siberian Railway later linked the region to wider markets. See Frontiers of Extraction.
  • East Asia: The Tang and Song economies, the Ming reliance on American silver, Tokugawa restriction of foreign trade, the Opium Wars, and Chinese Reform and Opening all mark shifts between openness and control.

extra.title: Debates and Limits
extra.html:
• The origins of markets and money stay disputed. Whether exchange began as gift-giving, barter, credit, or tribute is argued over, and the earliest written records, such as the tablets of Uruk, show accounting for obligations rather than any simple barter.
  • The size and reach of early exchange can only be inferred from scattered goods, and estimates keep changing. The extent and end of the Ghana Empire stay debated, and older population estimates for Great Zimbabwe of 10,000 to 20,000 have since been revised down to no more than about 10,000.
  • What even counts as trade is contested, because exchange, tribute, and coercion overlap so closely. The mita at Potosi, yasak in Siberia, forced rubber collection in the Congo Free State, and the Atlantic Slave Trade are all extraction, and scholars disagree about how much slave-based commerce actually contributed to industrialization.
  • Why Britain and Europe industrialized first, and why sustained growth began exactly when it did, stays debated, and the Industrial Revolution note does not settle the causes either.
  • This hub's coverage stays uneven. It has one note on a company (Dutch East India Company) and none yet on coinage, paper money, credit, or double-entry bookkeeping as institutions in their own right, and it has few notes on the internal economies of Africa, Oceania, and the Americas.
